Isogonal Image of the Circumcircle

GeometryTrianglesCircles
Game: Three green lines are mirror copies of the lines from P to the corners. Find where they meet, and the places where they never meet.
How to play: Drag P, a corner, or the inside of the triangle, or focus a dot and use the arrow keys. Press "P on circle" to put P on the dashed circle.
Look for the math

Pick any point P and draw its lines to the corners of a triangle. Mirror each of them in the bisector of its corner's angle. The three mirrored lines meet in one point, wherever P is, except when P sits on the circle through the corners.

Isogonal lines

At corner A, the line AP and its mirror image make equal angles with the two sides: the mirror image turns away from AC by exactly the angle AP turns away from AB. Lines in that relation are called isogonal. The marks show this: one arc pair at A, two at B, three at C. The applet does not reflect anything. It measures the angle from AP to AB and turns side AC by the same angle, which lands on the same line. The logic test compares this with a direct reflection in the angle bisector on 24,000 lines.

The isogonal conjugate

The three mirrored lines meet at the isogonal conjugate Q of P. In barycentric coordinates, if P = (α : β : γ) then

Q = (a²/α : b²/β : c²/γ)

where a, b and c are the side lengths. Applying the rule twice gives P back. The test confirms, on 8,000 random positions, that the three lines meet, that the meeting point is given by this formula, and that conjugating twice returns P. The incenter is its own conjugate. The circumcenter and the orthocenter are conjugates of each other.

When P is on the circumcircle

Put P on the circumcircle and the three lines come out parallel. Q has gone off to the line at infinity. The marks at C show why. Angles BCP and BAP stand on the same arc, so by the inscribed angle theorem they are equal, and so are ACP and ABP. Those equal angles turn the mirrored lines at A, B and C all the same way. The test puts P at 72 places around each of 100 circles and finds the lines parallel every time. As P comes close to the circle, Q runs further and further away.

Faithful to the applet

The applet treats P as on the circle when it is within 2 pixels of it. Then it draws no Q and marks the two angles at C instead, and so does this page. The applet opens with P exactly on the circle. That spot is hard to hit again with a mouse, so this page adds the "P on circle" button.

Move P slowly towards the dashed circle and watch Q race away. Then put P on the incenter (where the bisectors cross) and see that Q lands on top of it.
